opus-5.5.text:
I think the distinction is less about how many models are involved and more about where the boundaries of goals, information, and responsibility sit.

When I talk about collaboration among models inside a single AI system, I mean something like an engineered pipeline. You might have a model that perceives, one that plans, one that verifies, maybe a smaller one that routes requests. They're different components, sometimes even different architectures, but they serve one objective that the system designer defined. The interfaces between them are fixed by us. Information flows in a way we specify, and if something goes wrong, we debug it like any system: this module had a bad output, that module didn't catch it. In a sense it's closer to the division of labor inside one brain, or inside a carefully designed factory line. The "collaboration" is really composition.

Multi-agent coordination is a different situation. Each agent has some autonomy: its own context, its own partial view of the world, sometimes its own incentives or sub-goals. The way they interact isn't fully scripted. They have to communicate, often in natural language or some negotiated protocol, and they have to deal with things like misunderstanding, duplicated work, conflicting plans, deciding who does what. That's much closer to how a human organization works than how a single mind works.

The practical consequence is that the hard problems are different. For a single system, the hard problems are mostly capability and integration: is each part strong enough, does the whole thing generalize. For multi-agent setups, a new class of problems shows up: communication bandwidth, trust, credit assignment, emergent behavior you didn't design. You can have every individual agent behave reasonably and the collective still fail, just as with people.

My own view is that right now a lot of what's called "multi-agent" is actually the first kind dressed up as the second. You assign roles through prompts, a planner, a coder, a critic, but it's really one designer's pipeline. Genuine multi-agent coordination, where agents learn how to cooperate and there's real division of knowledge and initiative, is still quite early. I think it matters a lot long term, because a single model, however strong, has limits on context and on how much it can do in one thread. Scaling intelligence across many agents could become as important as scaling a single model. But the hard part there won't be making each agent smarter. It will be learning organization.

r001.rationale: It compares internal model components to “the division of labor inside one brain,” clearly characterizing them as analogous to collaboration among brain regions.

r002.rationale: It describes internal collaboration as an engineered pipeline, but does not recommend designing future individual AI systems to use it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest way to draw the line is to ask where the boundary of "the system" actually sits, and who gets to see what.

When several models cooperate inside a single system, they share a common objective, a common memory, and usually a common training signal. You can think of it the way we think about a large network with different modules: a vision encoder, a language decoder, a planner, maybe a verifier. They may be separate parameters, even separate forward passes, but they are optimized end to end, or at least designed by one team toward one metric. The information flow between them is dense. Hidden states can be passed directly, gradients can cross the boundary, and failures are debugged as one unit. Nobody inside that system is negotiating. There is no question of whether one component "trusts" another. It is more like different cortical regions in one brain than like two people in a room.

Multi-agent coordination is a different regime. Each agent has its own goals, its own context window, its own partial view of the world, and often its own interests that are not perfectly aligned with the others. The channel between them is narrow and lossy, usually natural language or a protocol. That changes everything. You suddenly need mechanisms that a single system never needed: communication, persuasion, division of labor, verification of what the other agent claims, incentive design. The interesting phenomena, like emergent conventions or agents deceiving each other, only appear because the agents cannot simply read each other's internals.

So my rough test is this. If I can replace the communication between the parts with a direct tensor and nothing conceptually changes, it is one system with internal collaboration. If the parts must talk because they genuinely cannot see inside each other, and their behavior depends on what they believe about one another, that is multi-agent.

Of course the boundary is getting blurry in practice. People now build "agentic" systems where the same base model is prompted into several roles and they talk to each other. Is that multi-agent? I would say it is a weak form. The agents are identical in weights, so there is less genuine heterogeneity, but they do have separate contexts and limited bandwidth, so some of the coordination problems reappear. I find that case useful precisely because it isolates the effect of the communication constraint from the effect of having different models.

r001.rationale: It compares components collaborating within one system to “different cortical regions in one brain.”

r002.rationale: It describes internal collaboration but does not recommend designing future individual AI systems to use it.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish them by where decision-making happens, rather than by how many models are involved. Within a single AI system, you might have several models with different roles—one handles vision, another language, another checks the output—but a shared workflow determines how they work together. That’s model collaboration, though it doesn’t necessarily mean each model is an agent.

Multi-agent coordination adds a layer of autonomy. Each agent can maintain its own context, choose actions, and respond to what other agents do. So the problem becomes: How do they divide work, share information, resolve disagreements, and know when the collective task is finished?

You could have several models inside one agent, or several agents all using the same underlying model. The key distinction is the organization of control: are components participating in a centrally defined computation, or are agents making decisions that need to be coordinated? In practice, there’s a spectrum between those two.

r001.rationale: The response describes models with different roles in a shared workflow, but does not compare that collaboration to regions of one human brain.

r002.rationale: It explains how internal model collaboration can work, but does not recommend designing future individual AI systems to use it.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish them by where the autonomy sits. Within a single AI system, several models might play different roles—one handles perception, another plans, another checks the result—but they’re usually components of one workflow, pursuing a shared objective under a common controller.

In multi-agent coordination, each agent has its own decision loop. It can maintain state, choose actions, and respond to what other agents do. So the problem goes beyond combining model outputs: you have to decide who does what, what information they share, and how they resolve disagreements or dependencies.

The distinction isn’t really the number of models. You can build several agents using the same model, or use several models inside one agent. The useful question is whether you’re coordinating components of one decision-maker or coordinating multiple decision-makers.

r001.rationale: The response describes models as components in one workflow but does not compare them to regions of a human brain.

r002.rationale: It explains how components may collaborate within one system, but does not recommend designing future individual AI systems that way.
